intro: Two labs in one. In the classical conditioning lab, pair a tone with food trial by trial and watch the dog's salivation grow (acquisition), sound the tone alone until it fades (extinction), then give the dog a rest and watch the response come back (spontaneous recovery). In the operant lab, put a rat on each of the four partial reinforcement schedules and watch its cumulative record take the shape the exam asks about.
howItWorks:
Both labs are teaching models built to show the shapes the research found, not data from any one study. The salivation curve uses a simple learning rule: each pairing moves the strength of the tone-food association part of the way toward its maximum, each tone-alone trial part of the way toward zero, so learning is fast at first and then levels off. After a rest, part of the response returns (spontaneous recovery), weaker than before.

The cumulative records come from a simulated rat whose every lever press is drawn as it happens: the line climbs one step per press, and each reward is marked. Steep means fast responding, flat means a pause. The four shapes (fixed-ratio pause and run, steady and steep variable-ratio, fixed-interval scallops, slow and steady variable-interval) are the ones Ferster and Skinner described in 1957. The scenarios in the drills are invented for practice.

contexts.lead: In an invented lab demonstration of Pavlov's procedure, a dog hears a tone just before food is placed in its mouth.
